title: When you only need to check that a related row exists (a semi-join), why is `EXISTS` better than an `INNER JOIN` — a join forms one output row per matching pair, so a left row with N matches is duplicated N times (forcing a slower `DISTINCT` to de-dup), while `EXISTS` returns each outer row at most once and can short-circuit on the first match?
shortTitle: Why EXISTS Beats INNER JOIN for Semi-Joins
topicTitle: Joins — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS

s1_definition.profdef: A semi-join returns rows from the left table that have at least one match in the right table, without multiplying rows. An `INNER JOIN` is not a semi-join — it produces one output row per matching pair, so a left row with N matches appears N times, forcing a `DISTINCT` to collapse duplicates. `EXISTS` is a true semi-join: it returns each qualifying left row exactly once and can stop scanning the right table at the first match.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India wants a list of accounts that have made any transaction. If you use an INNER JOIN of accounts to transactions, Rajesh, who made 50 transactions, appears 50 times in the result, and you have to run a DISTINCT afterwards to get him once — wasteful. With `EXISTS`, the clerk just confirms Rajesh has at least one transaction and lists him once, stopping at the very first slip they find.
s1_definition.oneliner: For "does a related row exist?", use `EXISTS` — it returns each row once and short-circuits, while an INNER JOIN duplicates rows and needs a DISTINCT to clean up.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A semi-join returns rows from the left table that have at least one match in the right table, without multiplying rows. An `INNER JOIN` is not a semi-join — it produces one output row per matching pair, so a left row with N matches appears N times, forcing a `DISTINCT` to collapse duplicates. `EXISTS` is a true semi-join: it returns each qualifying left row exactly once and can stop scanning the right table at the first match.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India wants a list of accounts that have made any transaction. If you use an INNER JOIN of accounts to transactions, Rajesh, who made 50 transactions, appears 50 times in the result, and you have to run a DISTINCT afterwards to get him once — wasteful. With `EXISTS`, the clerk just confirms Rajesh has at least one transaction and lists him once, stopping at the very first slip they find.

**One line to remember:** For "does a related row exist?", use `EXISTS` — it returns each row once and short-circuits, while an INNER JOIN duplicates rows and needs a DISTINCT to clean up.

sections.s2_technical:
An `INNER JOIN` combines rows: for every pair of a left row and a matching right row, it emits one output row carrying columns from both. That is correct when you actually want the matched data, but when you only want to know which left rows have a match, it is both wrong and slow. It is wrong because a left row with N matches appears N times — if Rajesh has 50 transactions, a `SELECT a.* FROM accounts a JOIN txns t ON a.id = t.account_id` lists Rajesh 50 times. To get the distinct accounts you must add `DISTINCT`, which forces the database to sort or hash the entire intermediate result to remove duplicates, an expensive extra step.

`EXISTS` expresses a semi-join directly. A semi-join returns a left row if at least one match exists, and crucially returns it exactly once regardless of how many matches there are. `SELECT a.* FROM accounts a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM txns t WHERE t.account_id = a.id)` never duplicates Rajesh and never needs a `DISTINCT`. It also allows short-circuiting: the engine can stop scanning Rajesh's transactions the instant it finds the first one, because one match is enough. On a large child table with many matches per parent, this short-circuit avoids reading rows that would only have been thrown away.

The performance picture: the `DISTINCT` on a join must materialize and de-duplicate the full Cartesian-of-matches, which grows with the number of child rows, whereas `EXISTS` cost scales with finding just the first match per parent. Query optimizers recognize `EXISTS` as a semi-join and often implement it with a hash semi-join or nested-loop that stops early. The senior guidance is: if you need columns from the child, use a join; if you only need to test existence, use `EXISTS` (or `IN`) so the planner uses a semi-join and you avoid the duplicate-plus-DISTINCT penalty. The same logic in reverse applies to `NOT EXISTS` for anti-joins.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants a list of accounts that have at least one transaction this month, for a statement-generation batch. A junior wrote it as an INNER JOIN and the batch processed Rajesh once for each of his hundreds of transactions, producing duplicate statements and running slowly. They added `DISTINCT` to fix correctness but the batch was still slow because of the de-duplication sort over a huge intermediate result.

Problem 2 — Rewriting with `EXISTS` returns each account exactly once with no `DISTINCT`, and short-circuits on the first transaction per account, making the batch both correct and fast.

Our mini-project builds an `ActiveAccountService` that computes active accounts both ways — the slow INNER JOIN plus DISTINCT, counting how many intermediate rows it had to de-duplicate, and the fast `EXISTS` semi-join, counting how many child rows it had to inspect thanks to short-circuiting — so the difference is measurable. It includes `Account` and `Txn` models, a repository where Rajesh has many transactions, the service, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three accounts — Rajesh (SAV2001) with four transactions, Priya (CUR3001) with one, and Amit (SAV2002) with none. Five transactions total.

Step 1 — The INNER JOIN plus DISTINCT approach loops every account against every transaction, forming a matching pair each time. Rajesh matches four transactions, so his id is added four times; Priya matches once; Amit matches none. The intermediate list is [SAV2001, SAV2001, SAV2001, SAV2001, CUR3001], five rows with duplicates, after inspecting all fifteen account-by-transaction combinations.

Step 2 — The DISTINCT step then collapses the duplicates into [SAV2001, CUR3001]. This de-duplication is the extra cost: on real data it means sorting or hashing the entire inflated intermediate result.

Step 3 — The EXISTS semi-join loops each account but stops at the first matching transaction. For Rajesh it finds TX1 immediately and breaks, inspecting one row instead of four. For Priya it scans until TX5 matches. For Amit it scans all five and finds nothing. Each matching account is added exactly once, so the result [SAV2001, CUR3001] is produced with no DISTINCT needed, and fewer child rows inspected overall because of short-circuiting.

Step 4 — Both produce the same correct set of active accounts, but the EXISTS path did less work and needed no de-duplication.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] === INNER JOIN + DISTINCT (slow: duplicates then de-dups) ===
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] active: SAV2001
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] active: CUR3001
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [WARNING] intermediate rows before DISTINCT = 15
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] === EXISTS semi-join (fast: once each, short-circuit) ===
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] active: SAV2001
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] active: CUR3001
2026-10-25 14:46:13 [INFO] child rows inspected (short-circuit) = 11
```

```text

    │    pairs: Rajesh,Rajesh,Rajesh,Rajesh,Priya  (duplicates!)
    │       │
    │       ▼  DISTINCT (sort/hash the whole intermediate set)
    │    [Rajesh, Priya]   ← correct but did extra de-dup work

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A semi-join returns the left rows that have at least one match on the right, without multiplying rows, and the key insight is that an `INNER JOIN` is not a semi-join. An inner join combines rows, producing one output row per matching pair, so a left row with many matches is duplicated once per match. At the National Bank of India, when we wanted the list of accounts that had transacted and wrote it as an inner join of accounts to transactions, Rajesh, who had hundreds of transactions, appeared hundreds of times, which produced duplicate statements and forced us to bolt on a `DISTINCT`.

That `DISTINCT` is exactly the performance problem. To remove the duplicates the database must materialize and then sort or hash the entire inflated intermediate result, and the size of that intermediate grows with the number of child rows, so the de-duplication becomes the dominant cost on large tables. `EXISTS` avoids all of this because it expresses a true semi-join: it returns each qualifying left row exactly once no matter how many child rows match, so there is simply nothing to de-duplicate and no `DISTINCT` is needed. On top of that, `EXISTS` can short-circuit — the engine stops scanning a parent's children the instant it finds the first match, because one match is enough to qualify the row, so it never reads child rows it would only have discarded.

So my rule is straightforward: if I actually need columns from the child table, I use a join; but if I only need to test that a related row exists, I use `EXISTS`, which lets the optimizer choose a semi-join plan and avoids the duplicate-rows-plus-DISTINCT penalty entirely. The same reasoning in the negative direction makes `NOT EXISTS` the right choice for anti-joins. In our statement batch, switching from inner join with DISTINCT to `EXISTS` both fixed the duplicate-statement bug and sped up the job, because the semi-join inspected far fewer child rows. The line I always state is that for "does a related row exist?", you use `EXISTS` — it returns each row once and short-circuits, whereas an inner join duplicates rows and needs a `DISTINCT` to clean up.

---

keyPoints: INNER JOIN: matching rows from both tables
LEFT JOIN: all from left + matching from right (NULLs for no match)
RIGHT JOIN: opposite of LEFT. FULL JOIN: all from both
CROSS JOIN: cartesian product — every combination
